Increased body awareness
Uplifting feeling in the body
Dreamy introspection
Mild and clear cerebral high

Strain Determines Effects

Some strains will have different characteristics than others. Therefore determining what strain to buy will determine the majority of effects you will feel.

Duration of Effects

Additionally, your previous history with cannabis and other intoxicants will affect the D8 experience, upping your tolerance level and possibly dampening some effects.
That being said, here are the possible times of the onset, peak, and duration of a D8 high:

If you’ve vaped Delta-8 cartridges or pods : You can expect the onset of effects to begin in about 6 minutes. Effects last up to five hours and the peak of the effects can be anywhere from 30 minutes to 2.5 hours in.

If you’ve ingested Delta-8 edibles or tinctures : This method takes a little longer due to the time needed to metabolize the compound. The effects may begin about 30 minutes to 1.5 hours in. It will hit you pretty much all at once. You may feel the effects up to 5 hours later, with the peak happening 1 to 2 hours in.
Once the high is over, you won’t feel drained or exhausted as with other substances. Simply a smooth come up, a chill buzz, and then a smooth come down at the end.
Possible Side Effects
Although a Delta-8 high can be a completely wonderful experience, it is also possible for some mild side effects to take place. As with any substance, there may be a few drawbacks. They are:
Increased heart rate
Reddening of the eyes
Muscle tension or tremor
Reduced motor control
Changes in visual or auditory perception
Time distortion
Difficulty in thinking, speaking, reading, or remembering

Typically these effects may happen if you take too much. To avoid this, start with small doses and work your way up to an amount that works for you. And remember that everyone is different. We especially recommend this tactic to first-time users.

If you are worried that you took too much, try to remain calm. Remember that the feeling is only temporary and it will pass when the high subsides. Find a way to relax by doing something you enjoy. This can be something like taking a walk in nature, watching your favorite show or movie, listening to your favorite music, or taking a pleasurable bath.
Effects Based on Previous Experience
As we’ve mentioned earlier, the type of high you feel may be based on your amount of experience.

If you are a first-time user : We recommend you be cautious. A first-time user is someone who has had no experience with cannabis products whatsoever, including marijuana or CBD. As a first-time user, it is important to start in low doses, working up to a level that is comfortable to you after each experience. This way you will not be surprised by any effects since you have no experience to compare it to. If you’ve experienced marijuana, you will have some idea what to expect. However, keep in mind that the high will be much less intense. But if you’ve only tried CBD products, Delta-8 can feel more intense. This is because CBD contains little to no THC, thus will have no psychoactive high. Therefore psychoactive effects can feel completely foreign to you. For first-timers, we recommend you are in a comfortable place. Make sure you don’t have any responsibilities to take care of, and that you won’t be driving. You will have a more pleasant experience the more relaxed you are. Take a small dose and enjoy!

If you are an experienced cannabis user : So when it comes to cannabis, you’ve been there done that. If this is the case, you will more than likely not be hit hard by the effects of Delta-8. This is especially the case for chronic cannabis users. Delta-8 is much less potent in comparison and therefore will be easier to acclimate to. If you are a marijuana user who is often overcome by the paranoia, anxiety, and foggy brain of THC, D8 might be the perfect substitute! You will enjoy more mellow effects but can still enjoy a fun body and cerebral high. Welcome to the Delta-8 world
Benefits of Delta-8 THC

With Delta-8, you don’t just experience these amazing effects. There are also a ton of health benefits that can come from this compound. This makes it not only a recreational substance but a medicinal one. A perfect combination.
The National Cancer Institute states that Delta-8 is “an analogue of tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) with antiemetic, anxiolytic, appetite-stimulating, analgesic, and neuroprotective properties.”

So, in plain English, you can experience effects like decreased nausea, anxiety, pain, and it can also bring back a healthy appetite. Additionally, there has been some evidence that Delta-8 can promote better memory retention and may help treat cancer. Let’s explore the research regarding these benefits.

Decreases nausea : Nausea occurs as a symptom of many disorders, as well as a side effect of many treatments. One of those nausea-inducing treatments is chemotherapy. In 1995, Dr. Raphael Mechoulam, the same doctor who discovered Delta-9 THC, discovered that after taking Delta-8 THC, children undergoing cancer treatment saw an improvement in their nausea and vomiting. These patients, aged 3 to 13, showed no psychotropic effects. Delta-8 THC is 200 times more effective as an antiemetic than D9. In some cases, it is 3 to 10 times less potent.

Reduces anxiety : People experiencing Delta-8 THC do not feel paranoid or anxious. Users report feeling uplifted and alert, yet still calm and relaxed. D8 is much less likely to induce anxiety in high doses than Delta-9 THC. This is an especially attractive quality for people who are using the cannabinoid for health benefits. Delta-8 interacts with CB1 and CB2 receptors in our bodies. It has been proven that the CB1 receptor in our endocannabinoid systems has a link to anxiety. When D8 binds with CB1 , it activates effects that promote relief from stress and anxiety.

Appetite-inducing : Patients experiencing loss of appetite from cancer and other illnesses have seen an increase in appetite, which allows them to get the vital nutrition needed. In 2004, a study on mice backed up these results.

Pain-relieving : Delta-8 has been shown to provide pain relief and reduce inflammation. In 2018, a study of mice with corneal injury under the influence of Delta-8 THC showed a reduction in their pain score. It also showed that D8 blocked the pain and had anti-inflammatory effects through the CB1 receptor. This showed that D8 could help treat ocular pain and inflammation.

Anti-cancer : In 1974, a study was conducted on the effects of Delta-8 THC on rats Unexpectedly, the researchers found that the cannabinoid had cancer-killing properties. There was not much follow-up research after this amazing discovery. The public is mostly unaware of the findings due to the decades it took for the government to admit the find. Studies on animals in 2006 showed evidence that D8, D9, and CBN may inhibit lung cancer. In 2013, the National Cancer Institute cited in a report that D8, D9, and CBD can stop tumor growth.

As it stands today, the research of Delta-8 benefits is still in its infancy. There is still a lot not yet known. Delta-8 continues to grow in its popularity, and we hope to see more and more research in the coming years. We will keep you posted.
Customize the Effects and Benefits

Knowing how cannabis can affect and benefit you allows you to customize it to your needs. Since the hemp plant comes in a variety of strains and is made of so many cannabinoids and other compounds, this gives you a smorgasbord of options to choose from.

As we’ve mentioned earlier, there are Indica, Sativa, and hybrid strains. Strains are made up of specific cannabinoids and terpenes. A great way to personalize your experience is to buy a Delta-8 THC product with terpenes. Terpenes are aromatic oil compounds found in cannabis plants, as well as other plants, that produce different scents and flavors. You can use terpenes to personalize your experience to your individual needs. Here are some of the most common terpenes:
Myrcene : This terpene is the most common one found in hemp. It smells herbal, musky, and earthy and is said to help calm and relax, as well as promotes sleep.
Linalool : Also known as the lavender terpene, this one has a floral aroma with a bit of spice. It is said to help reduce stress and promote good sleep.

Pinene : This terpene can be found in pine needles, orange peels, rosemary, and parsley. It smells of pine and is said to promote alertness and memory retention. Pinene has the opposite effect of linalool.
Humulene : You can find this terpene in hops, basil, and cloves, and has a hoppy scent. It is known for fighting inflammation and relieving pain.
Limonene : Found in citrus peels, this one has a natural citrus scent. It is said to help relieve stress and boost mood.

When cannabinoids and terpenes native to cannabis are combined, it produces an entourage effect. This effect is the theory that the components of the product work more effectively when working synergistically with other native compounds. This is because the product is mimicking nature.
So if you have the opportunity to consume Delta-8 with other cannabinoids and terpenes, the effects will be even more pronounced. Highly recommended.
Some other cannabinoids that assist terpenes to create an entourage effect with Delta-8 are:

Cannabidiol (CBD) : Hemp contains large amounts of CBD content, which is one of the most well-known and researched cannabinoids. CBD is popular because it has many health benefits, including help with anxiety, pain, inflammation. At the same time, it doesn’t have psychotropic effects.

Cannabichromene (CBC) : Though not as popular as other cannabinoids, CBC shows great promise in pain treatment. CBC is found in substantial amounts in the hemp flower, and when paired with THC, researchers believe it magnifies its analgesic effects.

Tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) : THCis present in hemp, but only in amounts of 0.3% or less. This is the same compound that produces the “high” that marijuana users experience. However, the low amounts in hemp will not produce a high. Even though THC may be highly controversial, it has proven health benefits. Due to these benefits, it is often recommended to be consumed in small amounts alongside other cannabinoids to balance out effects. Hemp provides the perfect balance of it all, in our opinion.

Cannabigerol (CBG) : Sometimes known as “the mother of all cannabinoids,” CBG is the precursor to both THC and CBD. This cannabinoid is showing a lot of promise in the treatment of various health conditions, but more research is needed. It may help decrease pain, anxiety, and inflammation.

Cannabinol (CBN) : Another compound found in hemp, CBN is known for its sedative effects. It is created when THC is heated and broken down and is one of the rarest cannabinoids in hemp. Even though it is created as a byproduct of THC, it is not strong enough to produce a THC-like high.
Get Your Hands On Some

Step aside medical marijuana, you have a contender. Delta-8 is an extremely beneficial form of THC that is giving weed a run for its money. And due to hemp’s newfound legality set in motion by the Farm Bill , you can now easily get your hands on some. You don’t even need to frequent the dispensaries to find it . Whether it be through the form of a vape cartridge, gummies, or distillate, we have the utmost confidence you too will enjoy the effects and benefits of Delta-8.

/blogs/news/how-long-does-delta-9-stay-i.text: How Long Does Delta 9 Stay In Your System?
If you’re a cannabis user or thinking about trying delta-9 products—you’ve probably wondered: how long does Delta 9 thc stay in your system?

Maybe you have an upcoming drug test for work, school, or sports. Or perhaps you’re just curious about how long THC metabolites linger in your body. The short answer? It depends! Everyone is different, and factors like your metabolic rate, usage frequency, BMI, and more come into play.

But don’t worry! In this article, we’ll explore how long Delta 9 remains detectable in your body using different drug tests, explain the determining factors, and give detox tips if you are in a hurry.
Let’s get started!
What is Delta 9 THC?

Delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol, or Delta 9 THC for short, is the primary psychoactive compound in the cannabis plant. It’s what interacts with your CB1 and CB2 receptors in the brain, giving you that classic high that cannabis products are associated with.
Depending on the strain, one may experience euphoria, relaxation, giggles, elevated mood, and munchies, to name but a few.

People enjoy Delta 9 in many forms, including nugs, edibles, tinctures, and vape products. According to USA cannabis laws, cannabis products that contain more than 0.3% delta 9 THC are considered marijuana and illegal, while those with less than 0.3% delta 9 THC, like THCA, CBD, and delta 8, are considered hemp and legal federally.
Does Delta 9 Show Up On A Drug Test?

Yes! Delta 9 THC does show up on a drug test because standard drug screening methods look for THC metabolites (like THC-COOH) in your system. These metabolites don’t leave your body right away, which is why Delta 9 THC stays detectable for a few days or weeks after the high wears off.
Here’s what happens:
You consume Delta 9 THC—by smoking, vaping, or eating gummies (or other edibles).
The THC gets into your bloodstream and circulates in your body.
It goes to your liver, where it gets broken down (metabolized).
The THC metabolites get eliminated into the intestines and bladder.
Your body gets rid of most of them through urine and poop.

But here’s the tricky part: Because THC is fat soluble, some of it gets stored in your fat (lipid) cells along the way. These fat cells can trap THC for an extended length of time, releasing it back into the bloodstream at a slow pace.

Even if you stop using cannabis products, your body may still have detectable levels of THC. And then there’s something called enterohepatic circulation. That’s where THC gets reabsorbed through the intestinal walls, gets back into the bloodstream, and gets stored in fat again.
Because of this continuous cycle, Delta 9 THC stays in your system longer after your last consumption. And that’s why it can show up on different tests even after several days or weeks of non-use.
Delta 9 Detection Times for Different Drug Tests
The type of drug test administered can affect the detection of delta 9 THC. Let’s take a look at how long delta 9 thc remains detectable by the most common types of tests:
Urine tests are by far the most common drug test for THC. Employers, sports organizations, and even healthcare providers use urine tests because they’re budget-friendly and reliable.
Occasional Users (once or twice a month): 3–7 days
Moderate Users (a few times a week): 7–14 days
Frequent Users (daily): 10–15 days
Heavy Users (multiple times a day): 30 days or more
Blood tests measure the active THC in your bloodstream, which tends to disappear faster than in urine. Thus, they’re used for roadside testing, accidents, or more immediate impairment:
For most people, Delta 9 THC is detectable in blood for 24–48 hours after use.
In cases of heavy or chronic use, it may show up for up to 30 days, but that’s rare.
Because it’s more invasive and has a shorter window, blood testing isn’t typically the first choice for routine screenings.
Saliva tests (also known as oral fluid tests) come into play when someone wants quick, on-the-spot results—like roadside testing in states where cannabis is still illegal.
Saliva tests can detect detectable levels of THC within minutes of smoking or ingesting it and are great for same - day use.
If you’re an occasional user, THC may clear out in 1–3 days . If you’re a frequent user, THC can show up in saliva for up to 29 days, but most people fall on the shorter side of that range.
Hair tests can be the trickiest if you’re concerned about long-term detection. When you use cannabis products, some THC ends up in your hair follicle through blood vessels and even sweat.
Up to 90 Days: Since hair grows slowly—about half an inch a month— hair tests can show cannabis use history 3 months ago.
Not ideal for Recent Use testing: It takes a couple of weeks for THC to show up in a new growth segment, so if someone used Delta 9 THC yesterday, a hair test won’t catch that yet.
Factors That Affect How Long Delta 9 Stays in Your Body
Keep in mind these are just averages. The exact time delta 9 stays in your body will depend on many factors like:
Frequency of use

The more often you use delta-9, the longer it will take for your body to clear it. Frequent users, heavy users, and chronic users accumulate more THC metabolites in their system than someone who uses it occasionally.
The amount of THC consumed also plays a huge role. A higher dosage means more delta 9 to process, which may extend the detection window in drug tests.
Each person’s metabolic rate is different. If you have a fast metabolism, you might clear delta 9 thc quicker than someone with a slower metabolic rate.
Body fat percentage
THC is fat-soluble. This means it loves to hide in your fat cells. The more body fat you have, the more space THC has to stay. People with lower body fat might remove delta-9 THC faster.
Hydration levels

It’s no secret that hydration helps flush out toxins. While chugging water isn’t a magic bullet, staying hydrated supports your kidneys. It may slightly help reduce detectable levels of Delta 9 THC in your system.
Method of Consumption

Smoking or vaping Delta 9 THC enters the bloodstream quickly. Edibles take longer to process since the THC goes through the digestive system. Thus, edibles may lead to a slower onset and a more extended timeframe before you feel the effects—and potentially a slightly longer detection period.
Delta 9 vs. Other Cannabinoids: Detection Time Comparison

Delta 9 THC isn’t the only star in the cannabis world. There’s also CBD (cannabidiol), Delta 8 THC, and THCA (the acidic form of THC). But do these other cannabinoid compounds stick around for the same amount of time?

CBD: Most standard drug screening doesn’t look for CBD, but some full-spectrum products may contain trace THC. If it’s full-spectrum, it could lead to a positive test result if enough THC accumulates over time.
Delta 8 THC: Chemically similar to Delta 9 THC but often reported as milder. However, standard drug use tests can’t distinguish between Delta 8 THC and Delta 9, so you may still fail a test.

THCA: This is the precursor to THC found in raw cannabis plant material. If heated (through smoking or vaping), THCA converts to THC. Detection times for THCA can vary, but once it’s converted to Delta 9 THC, it’s basically the same as any other THC product.
Can You Detox Delta 9 Faster for an Upcoming Drug Test?
Now, the million-dollar question: Can you speed up the process and rid your body of delta 9 thc more quickly?
Well, there is no magic pill to remove THC metabolites from your body instantly. Still, there are ways to speed up your body’s natural detoxification method.
Here is what we recommend you do:
Abstain and give it time: The best way to pass a drug test is to stop using cannabis as soon as possible. The longer you wait, the more time your body has to get rid of the out of your system.

Exercise: Exercise will burn fat cells and release THC metabolites. Running, biking, or even fast walking can increase your metabolism. Just remember that burning fat will temporarily release more THC into your system, so timing is everything, as you don’t want to do it right before a drug test.
Hydration: Drink at Least 2 Liters of Water Daily. Staying hydrated helps your kidneys and helps your body flush out waste, including THC, through sweat and pee.
High-fiber Diet: Fiber will move things along in your digestive system. It might reduce the chance of thc getting reabsorbed in your intestines. Fruits, vegetables, beans, and whole grains will help.
How long does Delta 9 remain detectable in a blood test?
Blood tests detect active delta 9 thc for a shorter detection window than other tests. Most users show detectable levels for 1–2 days, but frequent users might show positive for up to a week.
How long does a Delta 9 high take to wear off?

On average, the effects of Delta 9 THC last anywhere from 2 to 6 hours. But your tolerance, metabolism, and method of consumption (like vape vs. edibles) can change this timeframe. Edible gummies might last longer, around 6–8 hours.
How long is Delta 9 detectable in urine?

For occasional users, Delta 9 THC usually shows up for about 3–7 days in urine tests. Frequent users might see detectable levels for 10–15 days, while heavy users or chronic users can test positive for up to 30 days or more.
What is Delta 9’s Half-Life?

The “half-life” is the amount of time it takes to metabolize half of the Delta 9 THC in your body. This can range from a few hours to days, depending on factors like body fat, metabolic rate, and the amount of THC used. Generally, you’ll see numbers between 20 and 30 hours, but it varies widely between individuals.
Will Delta 9 gummies show up on drug screening?

Yes! Delta 9 gummies are processed just like any other THC product. The THC goes into your bloodstream through your digestive system, leaves its metabolites, and can appear on drug tests such as urine tests, saliva tests, or hair tests.
What are the legal implications for a positive drug test?

That depends on your local laws, the legal status of Delta 9, and workplace policies. Some places are more lenient, especially if you’re using hemp-derived delta or full-spectrum cannabis that’s legal under the farm bill.
However, many employers still have zero-tolerance rules. A positive drug test could result in disciplinary action or even job loss. Always check your local laws and guidelines.

Disclaimer: The information in this article is meant to be educational and does not replace professional medical or legal advice. We encourage you to talk to a qualified professional if you have concerns about drug use, testing, or wellness.

/blogs/news/how-long-does-weed-stay-in-y.text: How Long Does Weed Stay In Your System?
Are you feeling anxious about an upcoming drug test and curious about how long weed lingers in your system? You’re definitely not the only one!

For the most common type of drug test, which is a urine test, THC and its metabolites can usually be detected in your body for anywhere from 1 to 3 days if you’re an occasional user, and up to a month or even longer if you’re a heavy user.
The exact timeframes can vary quite a bit based on several factors, including your metabolism, how often you use, your genetics, and even the specific type of drug test being administered.

That said, stick around to find out more about how long marijuana stays in your system, what influences these detection windows, and some practical tips on how to detox naturally if you’re in a pressed for time.
Types Of Drug Tests And Their Detection Windows

When it comes to drug screening for marijuana use, urine tests are probably the most widely used option. They’re favored for their simplicity, affordability, and ability to detect THC metabolites even days after consumption.
Occasional users (once a week or less) may test positive 1-3 days.
Moderate users (2-4 times a week) may test positive up to 7 days.
Chronic users (daily or almost daily) may test positive for 10-15 days.
Heavy users (multiple times a day) may test positive for 30 days or more.

In some extreme cases, individuals who use marijuana very frequently and over a long period have tested positive for more than a month. This variation in detection times is largely due to how our bodies metabolize cannabinoids. THC (tetrahydrocannabinol) breaks down into metabolites that get stored in fatty tissues and are gradually released through urine and feces.
Hair Follicle Testing

If you’ve heard about hair tests, you know they have a reputation for detecting drug use long after the last use. A hair follicle test searches for traces of THC metabolites in your hair. Since hair grows slowly, these tests can reveal marijuana use that occurred up to three months earlier.
The detection window typically starts about a week or two after use when the hair containing THC emerges above the scalp.
It can detect usage for up to 90 days .

While this might sound intimidating, hair testing is less common than urine or saliva tests, mainly because it tends to be more expensive. However, some employers or specific programs prefer it since it can indicate a longer history of substance use.
Saliva tests (or oral fluid tests) are gaining popularity, especially during roadside checks. A mouth swab is noninvasive and easy to perform, but the detection times are shorter.
THC can be detected in saliva for about 24 hours for casual users.
For chronic or heavy users, up to 72 hours or more.

Whether you smoked marijuana, indulged in edibles, or just took a quick hit from a vape, saliva can show traces of it in the short term. However, these traces don’t linger for weeks like they do in hair.

While blood tests can be incredibly precise, they aren't typically the go-to for routine screenings. You’ll find blood testing more often in situations like traffic accidents or when there's a need to quickly assess impairment.
Blood tests can detect cannabis use within 2 - 12 hours after last use.
For chronic users, the detection window can stretch to 30 days in some cases.

Since blood tests focus on the active THC levels rather than just the metabolites, they’re more effective at identifying current impairment. On the flip side, other methods like urine or hair tests are more frequently used for long-term detection.

Though not as common, sweat testing is still utilized in certain scenarios. This method involves using patches that gather sweat over a designated period, usually between 7 to 14 days. It can reveal drug use that occurs during that time frame.
It’s often used in certain legal or probation situations where continuous monitoring is needed.
The detection window is how long you wear the sweat patch—so if THC is excreted through sweat during that time, it’ll show up.
Key Factors That Influence THC and Metabolite Retention in Your Body

Everyone’s body is unique, and the time it takes for marijuana to clear from different users can really vary. So, what factors influence how long THC metabolites stick around in your system? Let’s dive into a few key points.
Frequency Of Use

You know the saying, “practice makes perfect”? Well, when it comes to cannabis, “practice” means that THC and its metabolites can build up in your body over time. If you’re using it just once a month, your body will likely get rid of it faster than someone who smokes every day. Regular users tend to store more THC in their fat cells, which can lead to a longer detection period.
Method Of Consumption

The way you consume cannabis—whether it’s smoking, vaping, or munching on edibles—can impact how quickly it affects you and how long it lingers. Smoking or vaping tends to give you a quick rush of THC, but it might clear out of your system faster than edibles do.

On the other hand, edibles take longer to break down since they have to go through your digestive system, which can mean a slower release of THC and its byproducts, potentially extending the detection window.
Believe it or not, your genetic makeup can influence how your body processes cannabinoids. Certain genes can affect your metabolism, including how your liver breaks down THC.
Some folks might have a faster metabolism that helps them eliminate metabolites more quickly, while others may find themselves with a slower process.

Your body mass index (BMI) or overall body fat percentage also plays a role. THC metabolites tend to cling to fatty tissues. If you have a higher body fat percentage, there are more places for THC to hide, which often means a longer detection window. Conversely, someone with less body fat might clear THC a bit more quickly.

Staying hydrated can assist your body in flushing out toxins, including THC metabolites, through urine and sweat. However, don’t expect to magically pass a drug test just by chugging a gallon of water right before it. While proper hydration is beneficial, it’s not a foolproof way to ensure you’ll pass a test at the last minute.

Think of your metabolism as the engine that powers your body. A speedy engine can burn through THC and its byproducts much faster, while a slower metabolism takes its time. Factors like your age, gender, overall health, and even your mental well-being can all influence how efficiently your metabolic engine runs.
How Long Until the Effects of Cannabis Wear Off?

Being high is one thing; testing positive is another. The effects of marijuana typically fade within a few hours—about 1 to 4 hours if you smoke, and 8 hours or more if you consume edibles. However, just because the buzz has worn off doesn’t mean your body is free of THC. It’s like a shadow that sticks around even after you’ve stepped out of the spotlight.

While the high may be gone, THC metabolites can linger in your system, especially if you’re a regular user. That’s why it’s crucial to understand that the sensation of being high and the timeline for testing positive are two separate matters.
Again, the duration of cannabis effects can vary based on several factors, including your dosage, the potency of the weed, how you consumed it, and your metabolism, among other things.
How To Detox From Marijuana Fast

Now that you have a better understanding of how long marijuana stays in your system, what if you find yourself in a tight spot? You know, like when an unexpected drug test is just around the corner, and you need to get clean in a hurry!
Unfortunately, there’s no magic solution to instantly eliminate THC. However, there are a few steps you can take that might help speed up the detox process.

Stop Using Immediately: As soon as you think you might need to take a test, hit pause on your cannabis use. The shorter the time between your last puff and the test, the better your chances of testing negative.

Hydrate (But Don’t Overdo It): Drinking water is essential for keeping your body functioning normally and might help flush out some THC metabolites. Just be careful—guzzling water right before a test can dilute your urine, which could lead to false positives or raise suspicions.

Exercise: Getting active can really help burn off those fat cells where THC hangs out. Whether it’s running, cycling, or just taking a brisk walk, these activities can be beneficial. But a word of caution: if you exercise too close to your test, you might actually release some of that stored THC back into your bloodstream, which could spike your levels temporarily.

Diet : Eating a variety of nutrient-rich foods is great for your overall health. Some folks swear by high-fiber diets and certain herbal teas, although there’s not a ton of scientific evidence backing these quick fixes.

Detox Products: There are tons of detox kits available, each claiming to offer everything from instant cleansing to guaranteed results. The truth is, their effectiveness can really vary. Some might just temporarily hide THC metabolites, but there’s no promise they’ll work. Make sure to do your research before buying any detox product.

Give it Time : Honestly, the best approach is to let your body do its thing naturally. THC’s half-life can differ, but with enough time—anywhere from a few days to over a month—most of it will leave your system. If your test date is flexible, giving yourself an extra week or two could really make a difference.
Remember that no method is foolproof, but these pointers may increase your odds of a negative result.
How long will one hit of a cart stay in your system?

It's highly unlikely that one hit of a cart will stay in your system for more than a few days. Most sources will tell you the average elimination time after a single usage is around 42 hours. In some cases, depending on factors like metabolism or BMI, traces might be detectable up to 3-4 days after that one hit.
How long does thc stay in your bloodstream?

THC can be detected in your bloodstream for a shorter time than in urine or hair samples. If you are an occasional user, THC in your blood remains detectable for up to 24 hours and up to 72 hours if you are a heavy user.
How long does it take for marijuana to leave your body completely?
The length of time it will take for marijuana to be fully eliminated from your body will vary depending on many factors like your frequency of use, genetics, BMI, and overall health.
Occasional users might clear THC metabolites within a week, whereas heavy users could take a month or more to fully eliminate all traces. Hair tests can detect marijuana use for up to 90 days.
How can I pass a drug test?

It’s natural to feel nervous about a drug test. While there’s no 100% guaranteed remedy, the best tips are to stop using as soon as you can, stay hydrated, exercise smart, eat well, and, if time allows, wait out the detection period. For last-minute tests, some people turn to detox products or home remedies, but these aren’t foolproof.
How long do you need to be clean to pass a urine drug test?

The simple answer is “as long as you can.” However, for occasional users, 3-7 days should be enough to pass a urine test. Chronic users need at least 10-15 days and, in some cases, over a month to be clean. Very heavy or frequent users might test positive for up to 90 days in extreme cases.
Will THCa stay in your system like THC?

THCa is the non-psychoactive precursor to THC found in raw cannabis. However, once heated (via smoking, vaping, or cooking), THCa converts to THC, which can produce THC metabolites detectable in tests.
Can second-hand marijuana smoke cause a failed drug test?
It’s unlikely, but not impossible. Research shows that exposure to heavy second-hand marijuana smoke in an unventilated space could result in trace amounts of THC in your system.

/blogs/news/thca-vs-cbd.text: THCa vs CBD: Key Differences, Benefits & Effects
When cannabis comes to mind, most of us think of THC and the high it brings. But did you know the plant has over 60 other cannabinoids?
And now that cannabis hemp is becoming increasingly popular, two of those cannabinoids are now readily available on dispensary shelves and online stores: THCA and CBD.
If you’re considering trying either, you might be wondering what sets THCA apart from CBD and which one is right for you.
The main difference is that THCA converts into the psychoactive delta-9 THC when heated, and CBD is non-psychoactive even after heating.
If you want to get high, smoke THCA flower, dab a concentrate, or eat a gummy, but if you want to stay grounded, CBD will do.
THCa, or tetrahydrocannabinolic acid is the raw form of THC found in fresh cannabis plants. In this raw form, THCa is non-psychoactive. It won't send you to the moon.

The magic happens when heat enters the picture. When THCa is heated either through smoking or vaping or cooking it converts into delta-9 THC, that old familiar psychoactive compound everyone knows and loves.

This change is known as decarboxylation, and if you’ve ever made edibles, you’re probably familiar with the process of decarbing the weed first (by heating it in the oven) to activate it into THC before adding it to your recipes.
Chemical Structure of THCa

THCa has an interesting chemical structure! It looks like that of THC but with an extra molecule called the carboxyl group. This extra group makes the THCa molecule too big to fit into the CB1 receptors in your brain.
The CB1 Receptors are part of your body’s endocannabinoid system (ECS), which is responsible for regulating everything in your body, keeping mood, memory, appetite, and pain response in balance.
Effects of THCa
We’ve established that raw THCa on its own doesn’t have psychoactive properties.

But if you’re like most folks and plan on smoking, vaping, or dabbing your THCa products, you’re basically converting them into delta-9 THC on the spot. That means you can expect the same kind of effects of THC you’d get from traditional cannabis flower.
For example, lighting up a BaySmokes THCa pre-roll or taking a dab of some premium THCa diamonds might leave you feeling:
Euphoric or mentally uplifted
Tuned into your senses (vivid colors and music)

Of course, like any cannabis product, your experience will depend on things like your individual tolerance, how much you consume, and the specific strain you choose. Some strains have terpenes that will make you feel more energetic, while others will have you melting into the couch like a stick of butter.
Potential Benefits of THCa
THCa also has notable therapeutic and health benefits.
Anecdotal evidence shows that using raw THCA can help alleviate nausea, digestive issues, pain, and overall well-being.

Although research is still ongoing, some studies and clinical trials on animals suggest THCA might also offer benefits such as anti-inflammatory properties and antiemetic properties, which can help cancer patients undergoing treatment.

CBD or cannabidiol is a non intoxicating compound found in hemp plants. Unlike THCA, CBD does not convert to THC when heated . It won't get you high, but many people use it for wellness benefits like pain relief, stress management, and improved sleep.
In this section, we will explore the chemical structure of CBD, its effects, and uses.
Chemical Structure of CBD
CBD and THC have the same 21 carbon, 30 hydrogen, 2 oxygen atoms, but different arrangements, which leads to different effects on our body.
This is why CBD doesn’t bind to the brain’s CB1 receptors like THC does.
So whether you’re using CBD oil, edibles or tinctures, it stays true to its non psychoactive form.

As mentioned CBD doesn’t activate the CB1 receptor. However it’s thought to influence other cannabinoid receptors in your body including serotonin receptors that help manage your mood and GABA receptors that regulate your nervous system.
This is why CBD has FDA approval for certain epilepsy treatments, as it has anti-anxiety and anti-seizure benefits.
To sum it up, CBD works with your body to create a sense of calm without any intoxicating effects.
Potential Benefits of CBD
Because CBD interacts with many receptors throughout the brain and body, it’s used in medical marijuana for its benefits in supporting both mental and physical health.
Anecdotal evidence suggests CBD helps with:
Stress and anxiety
Faster recovery

Again, the effects will vary from one person to another. More human studies are needed to fully understand CBD potential. So far, the FDA has only approved one CBD-based medicinal product, Epidiolex (for certain types of epilepsy).
THCa vs CBD: Key Differences Compared
We have walked the long path! You are now well educated on the basics of THCA and CBD. Time to lay them side by side and look at their key differences (and Similarities).
Psychoactive Effects

In their raw state, both CBD and THCA are non-psychoactive cannabinoids. When you apply heat, THCA changes to THC and becomes psychoactive but CBD will remain non-intoxicating due to its stable nature.
Both compounds are hemp-derived and federally legal under the 2018 Farm Bill as long as they contain less than 0.3% delta-9 THC.
That said, some states have imposed their own restrictions on THCa because it can convert into THC. Still, you can legally purchase THCA from online sources like BaySmokes that ship nationwide.
CBD, however, is more widely accepted - which is why you’ll find it in gas stations, dispensaries, pharmacies, or any hemp store you can think of, to say the least.
Just remember, laws are always changing, so always check your local laws before buying.
Methods of Consumption
The market provides! You have plenty of ways to add either THCA or CBD to your routine. It’s up to you and what you’re looking for:
THCA products are available in THCA flower, vapes, gummies, pre-rolls, and concentrates
CBD products are available in oils, capsules, gummies, topicals (lotions, creams), tinctures, and edibles.

CBD is well tolerated by many but may cause dry mouth or drowsiness in some users. THCa, once converted to THC, can cause red eyes, increased appetite, and in rare cases anxiety or paranoia, especially if you make the rookie mistake of ingesting higher concentrations.
Choosing Between THCa and CBD: Which Is Right for You?
It’s a personal decision. It’s about what you want to feel and your wellness goals.
As a general guide:

Choose THCa products if you want psychoactive effects like delta-9 THC. This is for the person looking for a recreational experience, to unwind or change their mood. Just remember you have to add heat first.
Choose CBD products if you need balance in your daily wellness routine. People use it for chronic pain, stress or sleep issues.

/blogs/news/is-thca-natural.text: Is THCA Natural or Synthetic?
Yes, THCA or tetrahydrocannabinol acid is 100% natural! It’s a cannabinoid that forms organically in raw cannabis plants and is the chemical precursor to THC.
At May Smokes, we pride ourselves on offering only naturally grown THCA flower , unlike some brands that cut corners with synthetic additives.
It is, in fact, the most abundant cannabinoid in raw cannabis plants of the over 100 cannabinoids found in the cannabis plant.
Want to learn all about THCA and where to get some real natural buds you can trust? Keep reading!
What is THCA Flower?
Like many other plants, the cannabis plant produces flowers. When harvested, these flowers contain gland-like structures called trichomes packed with THCA, terpenes, and other cannabinoids.
So, in simple terms, THCA flower is cannabis buds high in tetrahydrocannabinol acid in its natural state, as it’s found abundantly in raw cannabis plants.
At May Smokes, we only source THCA flower that's been nurtured the way nature intended — free from synthetic sprays, chemicals, or artificial enhancements.

One thing to note is after harvest, cannabis flower with more than 0.3% Delta-9 THC is considered marijuana, which remains a controlled substance under federal law. On the other hand, those with less than 0.3% are considered hemp, which is federally legal under the 2018 Farm Bill.
Here is where things get interesting: remember how we mentioned that THCA is a non-psychoactive precursor to THC? When heated, it changes to THC, the psychoactive compound that gets you high.

This is precisely why you see many THCA products on many dispensary shelves. It is a sweet legal loophole in the cannabis industry. You can buy THCA flower and smoke it to experience all the effects of THC legally — and with May Smokes, you’ll always know you’re getting the real deal .
To dive deeper into what THCA flower is and why it's so popular, check out our full guide on THCA flower here .
How THCA Is Made: Nature’s Process, Not a Lab Product
One of the questions we often get is if THCA is man-made. The simple answer is no. There is no process for creating THCA in a lab.

THCA forms naturally as the cannabis plant grows—no synthetic processes are needed. We at May Smokes make sure to honor this natural process by only sourcing flower that's naturally rich in THCA, without chemical manipulation.
Earlier, it was thought that THCA was formed from cannabidiolic acid. Still, in the late 1990s, researchers discovered that its true precursor is cannabigerol acid (CBGA).
Here’s how it goes down in the plant:
The plant synthesizes olivetolic acid (the cannabinoid precursor)
Through enzymatic reactions, CBGA (the “mother of all cannabinoids”) is created
Then, an enzyme called THCA synthase converts CBGA to tetrahydrocannabinolic acid.
As the plant matures, the THCA accumulates in the granular trichomes of cannabis flower and leaves. These trichomes are those tiny, crystal-like structures that make good buds look frosty.

So, each time you look at a sparkling nug, you’re literally looking at THCA. The plant keeps these compounds in their acidic form until they’re exposed to heat—that’s when the magic of decarboxylation happens, changing THCA to THC, as we will see below.
Decarboxylation: How THCA Becomes Psychoactive THC
Like many other cannabis users, you may be wondering: can THCA get you high? Raw THCA is non-intoxicating, but it’s just one step away from becoming the psychoactive THC we all know.

When you heat up THCA through smoking, vaporizing, or cooking, you trigger a process called decarboxylation. Don’t let the big word scare you – it’s just THCA losing its carboxyl group (COOH) and becoming THC, just like CBDA converts to CBD when it loses the acid group.

Once this chemical transformation happens, the resulting THC molecule can now fit into your brain’s cannabinoid receptors and produce those psychoactive effects of THC we associate with cannabis – the euphoric high, relaxation, altered perception, and so on.

Around 87% of THCA in THCA flower converts to Delta-9 THC when heated. So, to estimate how much THC is in your bud, multiply the THCA content (which you can find on all May Smokes packaging labels) by 0.87, and that’s how much active THC levels you’ll get.
For example, if you had a bud with 20% THCA, after smoking, it would give you roughly 17.4% THC (20 x 0.87 = 17.4).
Transparency is key at May Smokes — we provide full lab results (COAs) with every product, so you know exactly what’s in your flower.
THCA vs Synthetic Cannabinoids: What’s the Difference?

We have cleared the air; THCA is indeed a naturally occurring cannabinoid. But it’s said where there is smoke, there is fire. So, when people talk of synthetic weed or cannabinoids, what do they mean? Is it even a thing? And if yes, how is it different from natural THCA?

Now, synthetic cannabinoids are definitely a thing. Products like Spice or K2 are artificial chemicals made in laboratories and often sprayed onto plant material to make them smokeable. These can be unpredictable and dangerous, causing severe side effects like rapid heart rate, psychosis, and other nasty effects, so it’s best to avoid them altogether.

In comparison, THCA comes straight from the plant itself. Some growers have mastered the art of cultivating cannabis plants with high THCA and low THC for legality at the federal level. After harvest, these plants go through lab testing for quality and safety before being packaged as THCA flower or extracted using solvents to create products like concentrates or tinctures.
At May Smokes, we reject anything artificial or synthetic — we’re committed to providing only naturally grown, lab-tested THCA products you can trust.

It’s worth noting that some cannabinoids like Delta-8 THC, although present in hemp, are in such low amounts that most of what you’ll find in the market is synthetic. Delta-8 THC is typically made from CBD through a process called isomerization to produce large quantities.

Whether you are looking for a high-potency indica, sativa, or hybrid, May Smokes is the place to shop. Order your favorite strain and enjoy discreet, fast delivery to your door. Is THCA safe to smoke?

THCA is generally safe to smoke when used responsibly and in moderation. Always source your THCA products from reputable brands to ensure you get lab-tested and organic products for a safe experience. For a deeper dive into this topic, check out our full blog on whether THCA is safe to smoke .
Is all THCA flower natural?
Yes, THCA is 100% natural and found in abundance in raw cannabis plants
Is THCA flower sprayed?
No! High-quality and legitimate THCA flowers are not sprayed with artificial coatings but rather grown naturally to contain high levels of THCA.
What are the benefits of THCA?
Smoking THCA has many therapeutic effects like relaxation, appetite stimulation, sleep aid, focus, and creativity.
How can you tell if THCA flower is natural or sprayed?

A natural THCA flower should have consistent trichome coverage, natural variation in color, and a fresh, complex aroma from the plant’s terpenes. Sprayed products will look uniform, have an unnatural coating or residue, and might smell like chemicals or have an overpowering artificial scent.

The best way to check whether THCA is sprayed is to review the COAs that should be made available with every purchase you make. On the other hand, if a cannabis product does not come with lab reports, consider that a red flag.
Is THCA legal in the USA?

Yes, THCA is legal at the federal level as long as it is derived from hemp with less than 0.3% data 9 thc on a dry weight basis. However, State laws vary, so always check your local laws before purchasing or using.
Does THCA get you high?
Yes, THCA gets you high when heated. Heat converts THCA to THC, which is responsible for the cannabis high.
THCA is the acidic, non-psychoactive precursor to THC found in raw cannabis. It has a carboxyl group that prevents it from binding to cannabinoid receptors in your brain.

THC is what you get after heating THCA, removing that carboxyl group, and creating a compound that produces psychoactive effects. They’re essentially the same molecule in different states – one before heat (not intoxicating) and one after heat (intoxicating).
Does THCA show up on a drug test?

Yes, consuming THCA products can result in a positive drug test for THC. This is because when you use THCA flower (by smoking or vaping), the THCA converts to THC. Standard drug tests look for THC metabolites, not specifically THCA, which can form in your body even if you ingest unheated THCA.

/blogs/news/does-hemp-have-thc-in-it.text: Does Hemp Have THC In It?

Hemp. Marijuana. THC. Cannabis. Sativa. Indica. All these terms may be confusing for first-timers to the cannabis world. No doubt you’ve heard of (or experienced) the psychoactive high of marijuana. But how does marijuana differ from hemp?

More importantly, does hemp have THC in it, the ingredient that produces a high? In this article, we will go through these terms, figure out what has THC and what doesn’t. This way you can know what to expect from your hemp products.
So, Does Hemp Have THC In It?

Yes, it does. However, there are only trace amounts of THC found in hemp. Having less THC is what distinguishes hemp from marijuana. Both are forms of cannabis with many of the same compounds in them, just in varying amounts. Let’s explore these differences.
Hemp and Marijuana
Varieties of cannabis plants have been selectively bred for thousands of years depending on the use of cannabis.
Some of these cannabis plants were purposefully bred for medicinal and psychoactive benefits. These varieties are now known as marijuana, their buds having THC levels typically averaging around 16%.
These plants are mostly illegal in the US for recreational use due to their high THC content. Many states offer medical marijuana, however.
Other taller skinnier varieties of cannabis were used for the fiber or seeds to make many things like:
Building materials

These are now known as industrial hemp and have low THC levels. Today these plants are being bred for their high CBD content and thus are used for CBD products. Many people enjoy these products because they are said to have a lot of health and wellness benefits, without the THC side effects. The differentiation Hemp has 0.3% THC or less, while marijuana has more than 0.3% THC. Since THC is what gives cannabis its psychoactive effects, this explains why you can get high from marijuana and not from hemp. Hemp won’t have these intoxicating effects since there are only trace amounts of THC. The 0.3 percent THC rule also determines the legality of the plant.

Due to the Farm Bill of 2018, hemp was taken off the Schedule I list from the Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) and Food and Drug Administration’s (FDA) Controlled Substances Act. Under this legislation, hemp and hemp derivatives are considered federally legal as long as they have 0.3% THC or less. Sativa or indica Both hemp and marijuana are part of the cannabis species. Typically cannabis is split into the subspecies Cannabis sativa L. or Cannabis indica. Sativa is said to be more energetic or uplifting, while indica is said to be more relaxing or sedative.

These two varieties are used as a basis for describing different strains, even though categorization has been debunked by scientists. The study examined the genes of 43 hemp samples and 81 marijuana samples. They noted that hemp is more genetically similar to Cannabis indica and marijuana to Cannabis sativa. But at the same time, the scientists noticed that marijuana and hemp plants still share very similar genetics.

This means that there are marijuana strains that are genetically similar to hemp and hemp to marijuana. It is the strain’s chemical composition that makes up the differences between whether cannabis will make you feel energetic, uplifting, relaxing, or sedative.

So now that we have sifted through the various definitions of things, let’s talk about THC. What is it exactly, and how does it cause a high? Delta-9 Tetrahydrocannabinol, or THC, is the most well-known and common cannabinoid found in psychoactive cannabis. It is found in high amounts in marijuana and low amounts of hemp.

THC is one of at least 113 cannabinoids found in cannabis. THC is similar to the natural chemical anandamide in structure, which is produced in the brain and is an agonist of cannabinoid receptors in the endocannabinoid system. THC binds to receptors and is then able to change normal brain communication. In this way THC will affect things like:
Sensory and time perception
Where is THC Found In Hemp?

Hemp is made up of stalks, seeds, leaves, and flowers. Where exactly is THC found? Both THC and CBD can be found throughout the sugar and fan leaves of the plant, but are mostly concentrated in the trichomes of the flowers. Trichomes are small resin glands resembling tiny hairs that coat the flowers. These glands are produced when the plant has entered its flowering stage of the growth cycle, to deter pests and herbivores.

Trichomes contain a higher concentration of cannabinoids, terpenes, and flavonoids than any other part of the plant. In marijuana, the trichomes of the female plant have high THC levels. Hemp has far fewer resinous trichomes.

You may be surprised to find out that THC is not only found in this form. It can go through many processes to transform into different compounds. These compounds are also present in the hemp plant (and even in our stomach). We will now introduce you to some of these forms of THC.

Delta-8 THC Delta-8 THC is another form of THC that has a less psychoactive effect. It is present in both hemp and cannabis in trace amounts, typically about 1%. Delta-8 THC is an aged form of Delta-9, thus the similar effects. When Delta-9 starts aging, the double bond moves to the eight carbon, turning it into Delta-8 THC.

Scientists call it a degraded form of THC because it is produced as D9 ages. Delta-8 is not considered part of the total THC calculated. Learn more about the differences between Delta-8 and Delta-9 THC. THCA The majority of THC in cannabis is in the form of tetrahydrocannabinol acid (THCA). THCA can convert to THC as the plant ages, dries, or gets exposed to extreme conditions in the environment.

Growers need to check the THCA levels of their crops before they are harvested to be aware of how much THC will contribute to their final amount. The Farm Bill mandated that both THC and THCA should be counted when a plant falls under the 0.3% THC requirement. The “total THC” means both THC and THCA, and this is properly calculated as THC + (THCA x 0.877). The reason for this, rather than adding the two amounts together is because of decarboxylation, the process where heat, time, or both convert THCA to THC.

The number 0.877 is used because it is the percentage of THCA that remains after decarboxylation. The result is the maximum amount of THC that could be found in the plant measured by dry weight. 11-Hydroxy-THC This is a potent, metabolized form of THC that your body creates after consuming marijuana edibles. Since it is THC in a different form, it can make the edibles seem strong even if you smoke marijuana regularly.

This is because when you digest THC through the liver, these metabolites can cause an increase in possible psychoactive effects. And even though this has become popular in the marijuana community, it is now picking up in the hemp community. Though CBD edibles will not have this effect since they don’t have much THC, Delta-8 THC edibles can form these metabolites once consumed. This means upon consuming a Delta-8 edible, you may experience effects 10 times more powerful than Delta-8.
Other Contents of Hemp
So what is hemp made up of besides THC and its variants? Here is a list of common cannabinoids, flavonoids, and terpenes that can be found in the hemp plant:

Cannabidiol (CBD) : Hemp has a high CBD content. CBD is one of the most popular cannabinoids because it has many health benefits, yet doesn’t have the psychotropic effects that THC does. CBD enables hemp products a high bioavailability, making them easy to absorb. Hemp flowers have some of the highest levels of CBD, so much so that the flower is often called CBD hemp flower or CBD bud. CBD is present in an average of 12 to 18% of the hemp plant.

Cannabichromene (CBC) : Though not as popular as other cannabinoids, CBC shows great promise in pain treatment. CBC is found in substantial amounts in the hemp flower, and when paired with THC, researchers believe it magnifies its analgesic effects. It is typically found in amounts of 0.2 to 0.3% in cannabis.

Cannabigerol (CBG) : Sometimes known as “the mother of all cannabinoids,” CBG is the precursor to both THC and CBD. This cannabinoid is showing a lot of promise in the treatment of various health conditions, but more research is needed. Though CBG is found in smaller amounts in hemp and is not well known, growers are producing more and more hemp varieties that have higher levels of it. A typical hemp plant will have less than 2%.

Cannabinol (CBN) : Another cannabinoid found in hemp, CBN is known for its sedative effects. It is created when THC is heated and broken down and is one of the rarest cannabinoids in hemp. Even though it is created as a byproduct of THC, it is not strong enough to produce a THC-like high. Hemp and cannabis naturally produce CBN in lower quantities: less than 1%. However, its potency will increase over time as it is exposed to oxygen or heat
Myrcene : This terpene is the most common one found in hemp. It smells herbal, musky, and earthy and is said to help calm and relax, as well as promotes sleep.
Linalool: Also known as the lavender terpene, this one has a floral aroma with a bit of spice. It is said to help reduce stress and promote good sleep.

Pinene : This terpene can be found in pine needles, orange peels, rosemary, and parsley. It smells of pine and is said to promote alertness and memory retention. Pinene has the opposite effect of linalool.
Humulene : You can find this terpene in hops, basil, and cloves, and has a hoppy scent. It is known for fighting inflammation and relieving pain.
Limonene : Found in citrus peels, this terpene has a natural citrus scent. It is said to help relieve stress and boost mood.
Quercetin : Found in green tea, red wine, and berries, this flavonoid acts as an antioxidant, anti-viral, and anti-cancer agent.
Apigenin : This flavonoid is found in parsley, celery, and chamomile tea. It is known for its anti-anxiety and anti-inflammatory properties.
Cannaflavin A : This is a flavonoid found uniquely in cannabis and acts as a strong anti-inflammatory.
Can Hemp Get You High?

The million-dollar question everyone wants to know: Since hemp contains THC, can it get you high? Hemp features THC only in trace amounts, so it is unlikely you will experience a high when smoking hemp. The plant is typically high in CBD, meaning you are more likely to experience non-psychoactive CBD effects.

However, if you purchase a hemp product that is high in Delta-8, you will experience a Delta-8 high. This includes things like Delta-8 vape cartridges, distillates, and dabs. Check out what the Delta-8 high is all about. So what about other hemp products?

Hemp seed oil : Hemp seed oil is an oil made from hemp seeds, not to be confused with CBD. It contains no THC and will not produce a high. However, it has a lot of nutritional and health benefits due to its large amount of essential fatty acids. It is great for treating inflammatory diseases, lowering blood pressure, and can even be used for skin care.
CBD isolate : CBD isolates only contain one cannabinoid: CBD. Therefore you will not feel any THC effects.

CBD oil and tinctures : Tinctures contain a range of cannabinoids plus 60 to 70% alcohol, while CBD oil is CBD mixed with a carrier oil. Either of these in a full-spectrum will include a range of cannabinoids and terpenes, including THC. Broad-spectrum CBD products will include the same components, minus THC. It is unlikely the full-spectrum products will produce any psychoactive effect since the THC is so low.
THC and CBD: Better Together

Studies suggest that THC and CBD work better together. For this reason, it is a good idea to buy a full-spectrum CBD product, rather than a distillate or isolate of a single cannabinoid. This is due to the entourage effect.

The entourage effect is the theory that all the compounds in cannabis work together, and when they are taken together, they produce a stronger effect than when taken individually. The phytocannabinoids and terpenes work together to create a synergistic effect that mimics nature. So if you have the chance to take a full-spectrum product, go for it!
Yes, Hemp Has THC

In this article, you’ve learned that hemp has THC in it, though only in trace amounts compared to marijuana. You’ve learned about varying forms of THC and all the other beneficial contents of the hemp plant. And you’ve learned that consuming hemp is unlikely to produce a high unless of course, you’re experiencing hemp-derived Delta-8 (wink).
